## Simple explanation

A metric is a measurement used to describe how well something is doing. In
machine learning, metrics help answer questions such as how often a
classifier is correct or how large a forecast error tends to be.

## Technical explanation

A metric is a function that maps observations, predictions, or system events
to a quantitative summary. Metrics may be computed over a dataset, a time
window, a user population, or production requests. The definition, unit,
aggregation, and population being measured are all part of its meaning.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Metrics guide model selection and operational decisions. A single number can
hide trade-offs, so teams often use multiple metrics and slice results by
important groups or conditions. Product and safety outcomes may not be
captured by a model-quality metric alone.

## How it works

Choose a measurement that reflects a decision or goal, define how it is
computed, and specify the data and aggregation used. For example, precision
measures the fraction of positive predictions that are correct, whereas
recall measures the fraction of actual positives that are found.

## Practical example

A medical triage classifier may be evaluated with recall for urgent cases and
precision to understand false alarms. The team can then choose a decision
threshold with clinicians, considering the costs of both error types.

## Common misconceptions

- A metric is only meaningful when its definition and evaluation population are clear.
- Improving one metric can worsen another or harm an unmeasured objective.
- Offline model metrics do not automatically predict the full production experience.
